speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the federal Government has granted an extremely unusual, if not unprecedented tax ruling to participants in the Gulf Canada takeover. Up to $1 billion in tax revenue is at stake in this issue. I believe it is critical for Parliament and Canadian taxpayers to know whether there was ministerial involvement in this tax ruling or whether the matter was determined solely by officials of the Departments of National Revenue and Finance. Parliament has a right to know whether the extraordinary tax break was the critical element in the Gulf takeover bid.
This tax ruling raises extraordinary matters of ministerial responsibility, concentration of economic power, and the appearance of fairness. I have repeatedly stated that the most effective means of attacking the federal Government's deficit is by a thoroughgoing examination of corporate tax breaks. This tax ruling is a classic example of my point.
1 have no doubt that the businesses involved in this matter acted within their rights, but it is not clear whether Cabinet Ministers acted in the public interest. The tax deal and the huge sums of money involved in the Gulf deal should be examined by Parliament in detail. For a business to seek a favourable tax ruling is perfectly legitimate. It is equally legitimate for Canadian taxpayers to know whether and why a tax break of up to $1 billion was granted.

Good news, Mr. Speaker. Canada's aging St. Laurent-class destroyers are finally coming out of the dry dock. They have been stranded for months while major refits have fallen further and further behind schedule. Now we know that the first destroyer will indeed be ready in time to take up its vital task in defending Canada-to be
scrapped or mothballed. That's right. The Government is spending $15 million to overhaul these 30-year-old ships at the same time as it is taking them out of service.
Won't Canadians be proud to know that their navy won't have to be shamefully towed to the junkyard? Instead, Canada's navy can hold its head high as its once proud vessels steam steadily on to the scrap heap. Can't you just see all hands on deck in their spanking new uniforms, saluting their commander as he hands over the keys to the highest bidder? Won't taxpayers be proud to know that the metal that gets melted down into their next Toyota will be taken from the finest fighting ships Canada can muster?
You would think that the Government would be proud of its latest effort to streamline Canada's navy and create jobs at the same time. Think of the benefits to the museums and scrap dealers of Canada. Why does the Government want to cover up this great success story?

Mr. Speaker, Canadians had a vigorous debate in recent months on Canada's participation in SDI. I welcomed the Government's decision not to participate. I did so for a variety of reasons, but primarily because I felt strongly that as Canadians we should set our own research agenda. I believe we should concentrate our research initiatives in areas crucial to our economic and social well-being; on things such as transportation, telecommunications and related aerospace systems, on health care, agriculture, forestry, mining, microelectronics, robotics, and our ability to live and work in northern terrains.
It is essential that we compete in the technological world of tomorrow. To do this, we must ensure that we have the scientific and engineering capability to be at the leading edge of future technologies. We must fund the academic and research components of our colleges and universities to ensure the future availability of those required skills, expertise, and new technologies.
Technology is one of our greatest engines of economic growth. Support for research is fundamental to establish a new era in science and technology to meet future challenges of our economic planning. I commend the federal Government for its commitment to exploit this opportunity.

October 2, 1985

Mr. Speaker, everybody, including the members of this House, knows that the Liberals, sadly bereft of Members and funding, can no longer afford proper research services. They have to rely on their instincts and the headlines in the media. That is the basis on which they are using, and will continue to use, the time of the House: by asking insinuating and insidious questions which mislead Canadians by camouflaging the real issues. The Liberal Government failed miserably on the important issues, specially those related to energy. And the few remaining members have failed in their role as parliamentarians.
During the election campaign, Mr. Speaker, we said that we intended to put the economy back on a sound basis and get this country out of the situation it was put in by the Liberals.
Today, the Globe and Mail published the following headline with commentary on pages B1 and BIO: "GDP grows 1 per cent during July". So far, since we came to power, the economy has outperformed the expectations of our forecasters. The output for 1985 will be 4 per cent higher than in 1984, and this will apply to all sectors: housing, manufacturing and durable goods.
Mr. Speaker, these statistics were published yesterday by Statistics Canada. I wish the Liberals would learn to read and comment on the important issues instead of indulging in this eternal nit-picking.

Mr. Speaker, it is my imperative duty to call the attention of Parliament and of the Canadian people to the unbelievable aggression of Israel against Tunisia which is located over 2,500 kilometres away from Israel. Not only is that bombardment an inexcusable aggression, but moreover, it is targeted against the most moderate Arab country whose President, Mr. Habib Bour-guiba, has advocated, since 1965 in Jericho, an approach different from that of every other leader in the region with regard to the fact of the existence of Israel.
Besides these tragedies committed against Tunisians, that aggression has jeopardized the peace process and the imminent negotiations between the U.S.A. and a joint delegation of Jordanians and Palestinians.
I do appreciate the condemnation issued by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) who stated unequivocally the illegality of that aggression.

Mr. Speaker, I am very sad to see that the State of Israel is getting involved in institutionalized terrorism.
Throughout the world, including in Lanarca not long ago, there are people who commit crimes, but this does not mean a Government should kill or mutilate innocent people as the Government of Israel has done in Tunisia.

subsubtopic: TAKEOVER OF GULF CANADA-POSITION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what is it about Petro-Canada that causes the Liberals to have such selective memories? Last December we heard the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) call for an inquiry into tax questions surrounding the PetroCan purchase of Petrofina. Today he calls for another inquiry. He showed no embarrassment that it was a Liberal Government, rather than a Conservative one, which gave $200 million in tax breaks to the Belgian owners of Petrofina enabling them to avoid payment of capital gains tax in Canada.
Now he is hot on the trail-after The Globe and Mail, of course-of the Olympia and York-Gulf-Petro-Canada dealings of last summer. He tells us that the partnership agreement between Gulf and Norcen to own and then resell the Edmonton refinery to Petro-Canada will cost the taxpayers millions of dollars. He selectively forgets that this artificial partnership arrangement, part of the corporate take-over game, was a Liberal tax law.
The Conservative Government gave special tax breaks to the Reichmanns to help them pay for Gulf, and Canadians deserve to find out just how much was given away and how. However, Canadians should also know that it was Liberal give-away tax laws which were used by the companies and the Government, the hypocrisy of the Opposition notwithstanding.

Mr. Speaker, this past weekend I had the privilege of attending a dedication ceremony of a new marine rescue vessel to be based in Sidney, in my riding, and named after Mr. Jack Simpson, the first westerner to be elected National President of the Power Boat Squadron and a founding member of the Marine Rescue Auxiliary.
Marine safety is a matter of growing concern for Government as even greater numbers of Canadians are taking to the
October 2, 1985

water for their recreation. Others have spoken in the House, and I identify with their remarks, about the need for increased funding of our Canadian Coast Guard. Frequently lost in this debate is the very valuable role played by the Marine Rescue Auxiliary, those men and women who contribute so generously of their own time and their own money so that all of us can enjoy our waters in greater security. I know that you, Mr. Speaker, and other Members of the House would wish to join me in giving recognition and expressing our gratitude to Auxililiary members like the late Jack Simpson for this important voluntary service.
As a footnote, I would ask that those involved in disposal of Crown assets give serious consideration to making available to the Auxiliary, at book cost, marine equipment judged surplus through normal replacement. In this way the valuable work of the Marine Rescue Auxiliary can be enhanced and expanded to provide even greater security to those many of us who enjoy recreation on the water.

Mr. Speaker, in recent weeks, several events have disrupted the lives of people in Mexico and the United States.
The earthquakes in Mexico and the damage caused by Hurricane Gloria, specially in the New England states, have once again given Canadians a chance to show their generosity.
Mr. Speaker, I would like the House to pay tribute to all Canadian men and women dedicated to helping those in need, and this includes Governments, public servants, relief organizations, rescue teams, workers and private citizens. I think it is only natural to congratulate those involved on the good work they have done in these and similar circumstances.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to pay special tribute to the teams of workers who agreed to go to the United States to help restore power supplies in areas that were badly hit by the storm. Hydro Quebec and its employees are doing fantastic work and are worthy representatives of our country. Thanks to their contribution, our relations cannot but improve.
Mr. Speaker, to all those dedicated Canadian men and women, I want to say: Bravo! and thank you on behalf of all Canadians who are proud of what you are doing.
Last Friday, Mr. Speaker, the CN announced 1,328 lay-offs in various yards throughout Canada.
Shame!

Not only are those job losses considerable, but Eastern Canada yards will be hardest hit by the lay-offs.
Two hundred and twenty-five jobs will disappear in Moncton, New Brunswick, including 73 as early as October 11 and the remainder slated to be gone by December 31. Mr. Speaker, the CN's decision shocks me and makes me very upset.
The fact is that Moncton CN yard workers got together last summer and forcefully demonstrated against the impending CN lay-offs. Through the Hon. Member for Moncton, the Minister of Transport had assured the demonstrating workers that he would speak out against massive lay-offs. There again, Mr. Speaker, the Government chose to betray the workers.
I therefore urge the Government to reverse the decision of the Crown corporation which has been insensitive to the plea of its workers. It has to realize that the loss of those jobs will have dire consequences in the Maritime Provinces.

subsubtopic: ANNEXATION OF VERDUN TO MONTREAL CITY
speechtext:
This coming November 3, Mr. Speaker, most of my Verdun-Saint-Paul constituents will vote in a referendum on Montreal's proposed annexation of Verdun.
Federal Members of Parliament have no say in matters such as this one which falls under exclusive municipal jurisdiction. Still, Mr. Speaker, may I urge all my fellow citizens of Verdun to become fully cognizant with all the implications of this important vote, particularly by attending the forthcoming public gatherings. I emphasize that as many Verdun residents as possible should vote in the referendum so that the voice of the people might be heard quite clearly, for the future of the City of Verdun is theirs alone to decide.
The simple fact that the Cities and Towns Act calls for a referendum when enough people are against annexation attests to the great significance of this decision and should be reflected in the interest shown by the people. I intend to follow the debate very closely, convinced as I am that the residents of Verdun will vote in the best interests of their community.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate this afternoon on the dissolution of Canagrex. When discussing the issue of Canagrex we should remind ourselves of the commitment that the Government made to the farmers of our country last year. When it came to making promises to the agricultural sector, the Tories did not spare any. They promised the farmers of this country just about everything. The Conservatives made no less than 20 different promises to the farmers of Canada. These are listed in the convenient booklet which I have entitled Three Hundred and Thirty-eight Tory Promises, which I think 1 have spoken to you about on a few previous occasions, Mr. Speaker. However, at no time did the Conservatives speak of the abolition of Canagrex. As a matter of fact, they promised to improve the farming sector. The Conservatives promised to establish boards. They promised greater assistance to the agricultural college. They promised to refinance farms and, as the Hon. Member opposite will know, they promised a farm review board and amendments to the Grain Stabilization Act. In other words, the Conservatives promised just about everything to the farmers of this country.
However, the first thing that farmers were subjected to after the election was a massive set of cut-backs. On November 8-
Canagrex Dissolution Act
a day which is normally known as "Black Thursday"-the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) launched his first hatchet job on the taxpayers of Canada with his massive cut-backs in agriculture and other sectors. One of those cut-backs announced in the statement of last November 8 was specifically the cut involving the Crown corporation of Canagrex.
During the deliberations of the Agriculture Committee last winter, members of the committee had an opportunity to interview the Chairman and members of the Board of Directors of Canagrex Corporation. We asked members of the board if they believed that this corporation would be useful, recognizing that it had been cut off by the Government in its embryonic stage. Canagrex had never been given a chance to get off the ground and seriously attempt to sell Canadian products abroad. Just as it was beginning, it was cut by a radical, right-wing Conservative Party which believes that the Government should not be involved in ventures like Canagrex. The Government believes that its Tory right-wing philosophy is appropriate, that is that farmers and others who are best able to fend for themselves will do all right while others will disappear. The farmers of this country do not agree. They have said repeatedly through the various farm organizations, such as the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the Farmers' Union, the Ontario Federation of Agriculture and others, that the Canagrex Corporation was never given a fair chance by the Tories.
Notwithstanding the fact that the Government is not concerned about those who are unable to manage at times without such assistance, it essentially broke its promise to the people of Canada. Not only did the Government break the commitments made by the Conservative Party, it broke those commitments made by the preceding Government when the Canagrex Corporation was formed. Many employees who came from the private sector and other areas of Government had joined that organization. In my opinion, that organization had a high level of expertise, with high calibre people who were well able to lead that Crown corporation and make it work to ensure that Canada has a good and strong international marketing arm in the area of agriculture.
During the last year we have witnessed deterioration of the agricultural sector. We have seen those involved in pork and beef production having to contend with greater international pressures. People in the beef industry are competing against imports from the European Community that are robbing Canadian farmers of their market. Pork producers in Canada were not only subjected to very low prices domestically, they have also had to deal with countervails from the United States of America against Canadian pork that was exported to that country. That has created a very difficult situation for Canadian farmers in the last year.
If ever Canadians farmers needed all the help they could get, including appropriate marketing tools, it is precisely now. At a time when prices are very low, we could use an expanded external market for our products. At a time when our farmers are facing these difficulties, a better tool for marketing our products could potentially bring higher returns.

October 2, 1985
Canagrex Dissolution Act
Let us examine what other countries are doing. When one watches television advertisements for such things as New Zealand spring lamb and other products coming from other countries, it becomes evident that those countries obviously have means by which they encourage the export and marketing of products from those countries. They have done it so well that they have now acquired world-wide reputations for the marketing of their products. Why can we not have that kind of vision when we have such vast agricultural potential with the commodities we produce and have produced so well in the past, even if it detracts from the right-wing principles of the Tories to refuse to accept Government involvement in marketing and other areas?
It is difficult to understand why the small amount that will allegedly be saved by closing Canagrex will not be used elsewhere in the agricultural industry.
I see the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) in the House. He is responsible for dissolving Canagrex and cutting the subsidies in other areas of agriculture. I understand that he represents a riding with a rural component and I am sure that the people of his riding are concerned about these massive cut-backs in an area of our economy that needs all the help it can get right now.
If the Government believes in the benefits of cutting back on agricultural subsidies and dissolving Canagrex, one must ask why the Conservative Party did not campaign on that theme. Why did the Conservatives not tell the farmers of my riding that if they voted Conservative there will be cut-backs to their subsidies? That certainly was not advocated in my riding by my Conservative opponent. Being the objective person you are, Mr. Speaker, I am sure you are faced with partisan rhetoric in your riding as well. Conservatives from across the country were telling farmers that the Liberals had not done enough for them and that only the Conservatives would rescue the farming industry.
I see the Hon. Member for Selkirk-Interlake (Mr. Holt-mann) here. I know he has a lot of farmers in his riding. I am sure if the President of the Treasury Board and other senior people in the Conservative caucus allowed him to speak he would say-I am sure he would because he is an honourable Member-that the farmers have been betrayed by the Tory Government. He is a Member who sits on the agricultural committee as I do. He would know that the actions of the Government have been most improper and have betrayed farmers.
There have been several other areas in which Conservatives have betrayed Canadians, such as for instance, in the area of farm finance, the agri-bond program which my Conservative opponent had put in front of my face during the whole of the last election campaign. Let me remind Hon. Members about the agri-bond program. Revisions to Section 31 of the Income Tax Act and the capital gains issue were three main issues in the election campaign of last summer affecting farmers.
The Conservatives, after the cut-backs of last November 8 in which they cut the Canagrex Corporation, announced at the same time that they would be releasing a Government paper outlining the reforms necessary to deal with the three issues I described a moment ago. When the so-called White Paper of the Minister of Finance appeared, it was nothing but a scathing attack on the farmers. It sort of said that farmers were well off and other such nonsense. You and I know, Mr. Speaker, that that is not the case and that the Government was not telling the truth, as has been the case of late.
The Standing Committee on Finance met and deliberated over this White Paper and issued a report. In that report, members of committee said there was a major problem in the area of farm finance. Not once did the committee recommend cuts; it recommended help. We advocated a system of agribonds, revisions to the Income Tax Act, as well as the complete removal of capital gains for farms that were to be used only for farmland in the future. What happened, Mr. Speaker? We heard of the removal of capital gains for everybody, including those who wanted to sell yachts, castles in Spain, horses in Kentucky and other things. This will only partly assist farmers but it will benefit the rich investing in all kinds of other things that I have described.
In terms of meaningful assistance to keep farmers in the farming business, there was not word in the Budget of the Minister of Finance. The only thing the Minister of Finance has stated, along with his friend "Erik the Dreaded"-the Minister in charge of cut-backs-the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen), a further set of cuts in the agricultural sector to condense and streamline, which is a euphemism for cut, other Government programs.
Farmers in my constituency after the Budget met through their local federation of agriculture and issued a resolution condemning the Budget. I presented that resolution in the House. I am sure you recall it vividly, Mr. Speaker, that resignation called upon the Minister of Finance to come to his senses and help the farmers the way the Conservatives promised last summer. It called upon the Conservatives not to keep cutting various programs, like Canagrex and other meaningful programs established by the previous Liberal Government. In so doing, we all hoped that the Minister of Finance, when he changed his mind on that other disaster in which he got himself involved-the cuts to senior citizen's pensions-would have the good sense to say, "I just did not make one mistake, I made more than one", and would take the golden opportunity to backpeddle and announce that he was going to inject a fair amount of funds into the agricultural sector. We hoped he would see the light and restore Canagrex, allowing it to function, and at least giving it a chance to market Canadian products internationally.
Farmers are feeling more and more the very difficult financial situation in which they find themselves. More and more they feel betrayed by a Government that promised during an election campaign that it would do major things to help out their industry. More and more farmers are going under. Pork producers in the constituency that I represent issued a resolu-
October 2, 1985

tion the other day that I want to read into the record. This motion was sent to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise). It reads:
The Prescott County Pork Producers' Association requests that a national referendum be held in order to allow individual pork producers to freely express their opinion on the subject of supply management in their industry, all this in conformity with pledges made by the federal Government.
Further we wish to inform the authorities that they reject all systems that would not take into account regional disparities regarding the costs of production, and we reaffirm our solidarity with the arguments raised by the Federation des Producteurs de Pores du Quebec and by the Pork Producers Association of Ontario, such as Bruce County and others.
Clearly pork producers on supply management have asked for help. They want protection to ensure they have good prices. They do not want to be rich. They only want to have a decent living. Canagrex could have assisted in the international marketing of their products and, hopefully, provided to them that decent standard of living, which is all they were asking for, but again they have been betrayed by this Government.

Mr. Speaker, although the Hon. Member talked very clearly about the farmers, I do not believe he indicated how this lack of an agency would have an impact on his riding in particular, either in terms of what kinds of products are produced-and I am not that familiar with his riding-or in terms of consumers in his area and of not being able to have a full market abroad to sell agricultural products that would ensure a reasonable rate for products in Canada.

Let me thank the Hon. Member for his question, Mr. Speaker. Much of the agricultural industry in Glengarry-Prescott-Russell consists of dairy, pork, beef, potatoes, some livestock feed, cereals and corn. By and large, that industry in my constituency is suffering quite a bit. Perhaps dairy producers are not suffering as much as others. Only a few years ago there was the view that a dairy producer did well. Now it is said that a dairy producer is not quite as badly off. It is a far different story from what it used to be. Nevertheless, others are worse off than dairy producers.
In fact, pork producers are the worst off. Recently we saw how being dependent on only one international market can affect that industry. I draw the attention of the House to the threat of and the subsequent countervail by the United States of America against pork products which we sell abroad. That countervail had the effect of reducing the price of Canadian pork. It also had a depressing effect upon the market. Prices went down somewhere in the area of twice the countervail rate. That countervail rate varied between 3.5 cents and a little over 5 cents per pound, but the depressing effect of the countervail on the market was almost twice that amount. It understandably created a form of panic in the industry. People were wondering what would happen, whether there would be subsequent increases in the countervail charge and so on.
I recognize that the area which I represent is a part of Ontario where the cost of pork production is greater than in other areas. The southwestern part of the province produces pork for perhaps 4 cents to 5 cents per pound cheaper. Of
Canagrex Dissolution Act
course there are differences, depending upon the specific way in which individuals run their farming operations. Eastern Ontario already had a smaller profit margin because of higher freight costs, food costs and so on. Therefore that countervail duty resulted in an even further loss. In other words, the disaster was accelerated.
In direct response to the Hon. Member's question let me say that if we had a good, strong network to market agricultural products world-wide, we would not be so dependent upon one market and we would be able to sell more. Those are not my comments; those are the comments of representatives of various agricultural federations who appeared before the Standing Committee on Agriculture. Of all the groups which appeared, none subscribed to the view that Canagrex should be abolished.
If the Conservatives purport to speak for Canadian farmers, how can they reconcile closing down Canagrex when there is not one agricultural group, of which I know, that agrees with their view? One can only conclude that it is the philosophical view of the Conservatives to get out of this business or not to be involved. It is unusual that they have a different view when it comes to bailing out some of their rich friends such as bankers and other groups in society like people purchasing oil companies, as we saw last week. Of course that will involve an expenditure far greater than the cost of the retention of Canagrex. Now we know the priorities of the Government.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot help but rise to make a few comments on the speech of the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) and his idea that he knew what I would say regarding the termination of Canagrex. Apparently he knew how I felt about my Party. He indicated that I would condemn my Party for taking the actions it has taken. I tell the Hon. Member that I support the termination of Canagrex. In fact, the producers and farmers of my area do as well. They did not like seeing another glorified, bureaucratic, very expensive nightmare organization which had no idea as to what it would sell, where it would sell, when it would sell or any such thing. The Hon. Member seems to think that it was a miracle for farmers. From where did he get that dreamy, "schemey" idea? It was never indicated in the formation of Canagrex what it was able to accomplish, although a lot of money was assigned to the things it might be able to do. The Hon. Member used broad statements. He said that it would probably make farmers rich and that it would be their salvation. Can you believe that, Mr. Speaker? Also he said that we should have given it a chance.
The past administration cost Canadians billions of dollars. We were close to $180 billion in debt as a result of giving such programs a chance and we had the highest unemployment rate ever. That is the Liberal idea of trying another program. Instead of only $180 billion, I suppose we would have hit the $250 billion mark by now, had they still been in power. That is the reason for the attitude of the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell not having any merit in form. It is the typical attitude. He decided what I thought about the particular Bill. He must be a soothsayer. Perhaps he would have predicted the

Ides of March, had he had the chance. I just wanted to clarify his statements about what I thought.

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of State (Canadian Wheat Board)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, certainly it is a pleasure to speak on behalf of the Government on Bill C-77. I think a couple of things need to be said. Needless to say, Mr. Speaker, with a name like I have, I think it is entirely appropriate that I should speak to this Bill. Aside from that, though, I have had a fair amount to do with horses and at least a little to do with racing.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I believe one of the things of which Canadians are not generally aware is the size and importance of the racing industry. It is an extremely large industry which generates in the neighbourhood of $1.5 billion a year. It employs something like 40,000 permanent employees and, according to the figures I have, approximately 13 million people attended at race-tracks last year which is more than the attendance at professional hockey, football and baseball games put together. I am sure that a lot of people are unaware of the size and significance of this industry.
It is also very much of a renewable resource. What we are attempting to do today is to pass some amendments to the Act which is presently in place which will provide for a better operation for everyone concerned.
The changes are designed to stimulate the economic health of all segments of the racing industry in Canada, and to ensure fair racing for the betting public. To enhance the marketing power of the sector, we would permit Canadians to place legal bets in Canada on foreign races such as the popular and prestigious Kentucky Derby, the Belmont Stakes, the Preak-ness and others and, when feasible, important races in Europe and even in Japan. I want to assure Hon. Members that because we will permit betting on foreign races, we will not in any way relax Canada's stringent drug control standards. The number and quality of foreign races offered to Canadian bettors will be regulated to ensure that betting on races abroad does not displace live racing in Canada.
All money bet on foreign races will stay in Canada. It will increase revenues for both the tracks, the horsemen and, through them, all sectors of the industry. Racing associations will be able to set and adjust the percentage of the betting dollar they deduct up to the level established in regulations. Most associations split these revenues with the horsemen as prize money on a fifty-fifty basis.
To provide more comfort and convenience for the public, racing associations will be permitted to use other buildings on their property adjacent to the track for the purposes of parimutuel betting. In addition, they will be permitted to broadcast their own races and associated betting data live on television. The change will remove the uncertainty as to the legality of this common practice.
I want to assure those who may feel that the Government is in any way encouraging gambling, that by legalizing betting on foreign races, we are ensuring that the revenues which at present have the potential to leave Canada, will stay in Canada to help support the industry.
The proposed changes will also discourage illegal bookmaking. Such betting will contribute to provincial and federal tax revenues through the taxes paid by racing associations. The federal levy, not to exceed 1 per cent on all bets, remains constant. Agriculture Canada's racetrack division conducts all drug testing on horses, videotapes of all pari-mutuel races, and carries out other necessary racetrack supervision to ensure
October 2, 1985

protection for the public on a complete cost recovery basis financed by the levy.
Other amendments to Section 188 to bring regulations into line with modern communications technology and veterinary practices. For example, videotape will replace film as the medium for recording races as an aid to officials.
Tests on other bodily substances such as blood will be officially added to the urine and saliva tests conducted routinely on all racehorses. Regulations will now allow analysis of body tissues from horses which die immediately before, during or after a race.
Other clarifications include the definition of a racing association as an association which actually conducts horseracing, and not merely has racing as its purpose, or one of its purposes. Essentially, these changes are good housekeeping. They are designed to ensure that our legalization reflects reality, protects the public and does not inhibit the viability and potential of the industry.
Race-tracks, as I said, are important economic generators in many of the smaller communities right across the country. I think it is important to mention, Mr. Speaker, that we have racing basically throughout the country, especially during the summer season when there are a lot of smaller fairs which have, as part of their attraction, pari-mutuel betting. Those are my comments on second reading, thank you.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-77, which is before us today, is designed to expand the arrangements for betting at Canadian race-tracks, to provide for broadcasts of races taking place in the United States or in other countries and to allow betting on them here in Canada.
I think that people who are concerned about gambling could well be concerned that this will actually increase the amount of gambling which takes place in our country. However, I think we have to balance that with the prospect that this will be gambling under a controlled situation at Canadian racetracks rather than people going to the United States. I am told that something like $157,000 was wagered on the Kentucky Derby by Canadians. It has been found that on important race days in the United States, the number of people attending our race-tracks is dramatically reduced. As the Minister indicated, there are something like 40,000 people involved in the race-track industry, and it is one of the major sporting events in the country.
This legislation before us today would provide for the broadcasts of races in other countries at tracks in Canada at a time when live races are taking place here. I have been assured by the Department of Agriculture that this will be a controlled situation and that there will be regulations as to the number of races which are carried in this way.
I also believe it is important that the legislation which now exists is tied in to meet modern day standards with regard to the use of videotape as opposed to fdm, and with respect to the technical aspect of blood tests and body fluid tests which are carried out on the racehorse. I believe the Department of Agriculture which regulates these horse races which are tele-
Criminal Code
vised, must take into account the over-all impact on the nearby tracks. For instance, I am told that when live races are carried on television in Toronto, it does have a negative impact on the turnout at the Five tracks involved in the jockey club. So I think it is important there be some equity exercised in the operation of this inter-track racing arrangement which would now take place.
I believe those are the only items which I want to mention. I understand that the Minister is going to be proposing amendments at the committee of the whole stage. I hope he will be able to explain the provisions of that amendment. So with those few comments, Mr. Speaker, may I say that we are agreeable to see this Bill passed through committee of the whole stage.

Mr. Speaker, I want to speak on the "sin" Bill. It reminds me of a story of a chap who was at a race-track. He was standing in the pari-mutuel line to buy a ticket. He was at the $100 win window. There were six horses in the race. He said to the clerk at the window, "I want to put $500 on number six to win". The teller cranked out the ticket, but the fellow behind him tapped him on his shoulder and said, "Look, buddy, number six is not going to win." The guy said, "Oh, yeah?" So he said to the clerk, "Give me another 500 bucks on number six to win." The guy taps him on the shoulder again and says, "Look, what's the matter with you? Are you crazy? Number six can't win". The guy says, "Yeah? Give me another 500 bucks on number six to win". The other guy got completely frustrated and said, "Look, I own number six and I have told the jockey we're only out for a ride today". The guy turned around and said, "Well, this is going to be one heck of a slow race. I own the other five".
Oh, oh!
Mr. Speaker, I do not want my remarks to be interpreted as those of a socialist arguing for sin.

We were waiting to see what you were going
to do.

I do not want it to appear as though we socialists who believe in economic planning would depend upon the exigencies of betting. I would like to lay odds of Five to one that Members of the House cannot tell me what the Government will get on the 1 per cent on foreign races on which Canadians will bet.
I am not here to argue that betting is an essential source of income for the Government. However, I think pari-mutuel betting and horse racing in Canada is a civilized and accepted form of recreation. There is no doubt about that. Indeed, as far as I can tell, what this Bill attempts to do is to modernize betting to make sure that the regulations controlling it are in fact up to modern standards. These things include what happens when a horse drops dead after it Finishes a race. It provides that we can examine body parts of the animal rather

October 2, 1985
Criminal Code
than do only urine or blood tests to detect foreign substances. Indeed, for some horses it does not matter. One can give them anything but there is no way they will win.
I do not think that I could oppose this Bill. After all, there is a race-track in my riding.
Conflict of interest?

Not at all. Indeed, it is a small "B" track which operates two days a week. In fact, it provides employment opportunities not only for those who are trainers but also for those with few skills. There are very few other opportunities for employment in that regard.
It will be possible for a track like the one to which I just referred to broadcast foreign races of a premier standard including the Kentucky Derby, the English Derby, the Grand National, the Belmont Stakes and the Preakness. I think that Canadians who want to place bets on those races ought to be able to do so at a facility in Canada. I do not think they should have to shuffle off to Buffalo to off-track bet on races occurring in the United States on which they cannot bet in Canada. I think we are now recognizing that betting here is a civilized thing and that such facilities should be available to Canadians.
The other day as I was preparing for this debate, I recognized the considerable investment there is in horse breeding and racing in Canada. For example, in 1983, investment capital in the race-track business was $2.2 billion. We have a surplus trade balance with the United States regarding the whole question of breeding and selling horses. For example, no one can forget Northern Dancer who, at 24 or 25 years of age, still services about 16 mares every year. In fact, all of his offspring has made Northern Dancer, a Canadian-bred stallion, the world's most famous stallion.
We must recognize, Mr. Speaker, that E. P. Taylor did not achieve all of that simply by pulling himself up by his own bootstraps. The provincial Government of Ontario made grants available to horse breeders to improve the breed and to make Canadian-bred horses very attractive to foreign markets. As a matter of fact, through the Income Tax Act under the agricultural section, the federal Government provides tax relief for those who are involved in the businesses of the breeding and racing of horses. I believe that we are Finally becoming more civilized with respect to the way we respond to the entire question of horse racing.
One good aspect of this Bill, of course, is the possibility that it would eliminate bookmaking. Bookies take bets and if they get too many heavy bets on one horse in a particular race, they lay them off on bookies in Buffalo or elsewhere in the United States. This Bill will effectively put the run on that kind of illegal activity, activity which is a part of organized crime. That is a step in the right direction.
We are not prepared to oppose this Bill. When it gets to committee of the whole, there are, however, some questions I would like to ask vis-a-vis betting on races across Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to add a few words to this discussion because I am
sure all of us are very conscious of the considerable number of Canadians who may be troubled by this kind of legislation. I think it is very important for the Parliament of Canada, particularly when there is all-Party support, to indicate why this kind of legislation is desirable.
This legislation certainly does not point to an indifference on the part of this Parliament to the moral problem that is faced by many compulsive gamblers, a problem which brings great unhappiness and misery to their families and dependants. However, we also know that there is very little good that comes from the law being used to prohibit and to restrain. There is, however, real good to be achieved from the law being used to control, to ensure honesty and wholesomeness and to ensure the fairness of the facility for all Canadians who wish to participate. I take it that that is the intent of this legislation.
On the negative side, I have some concern that this legislation, like so much legislation in the various provinces and in Parliament, still gives considerable weight to the interests of the major race tracks and confines its benefits to race tracks and the pari-mutuel facilities. There is some argument for that. However, I doubt that the expectations of the Hon. Member for Sudbury (Mr. Rodriguez) regarding the elimination of bookmaking will be fulfilled because of the limitations of this legislation. Notwithstanding that, these amendments are taking us a step forward, and perhaps at a later time we can consider a further step that will provide more facilities for the people of Canada who have an interest in this sport.

speechtext:
Order. House in Committee of the Whole on Bill C-77, an Act to amend the Criminal Code (parimutuel betting).
On Clause 1-

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the Minister what sort of regulations he envisions being put in place to regulate the number of races which will be permitted to be used for this purpose which originate from outside the country.
October 2, 1985

I am sure it is not the intention of the Government to supplant the races which are taking place in Canada at the present time. While everyone knows the Kentucky Derby and similar races hold a great attraction, there are also many other famous races which take place in Europe and other countries. What sort of regulations does the Minister envision being put in place to prevent an over-abundance of races from outside the country?

Mr. Chairman, the Hon. Member raises a valid question. The number of races held will be strictly limited by regulations set by the Minister. Presently, the number being considered is 40, which does not mean races held on 40 different days but 40 different races. For example, if we consider the Breeder Stakes to be held this fall, on one day there will be 10 races covered. We are certainly not looking to a proliferation of races whereby Canadians will be allowed to bet on every race held anywhere. We are talking about the prestigious races. If we consider the number 40, then I believe that would satisfy most people with respect to the concern suggested by the import of the Hon. Member's question.
r

Mr. Chairman, will the Minister indicate to the Committee of the Whole what percentage of winnings will be returned in the case of foreign races? Will it be the same formula which we have in place for domestic races or will it be a larger amount? A larger amount would give some sort of preference to Canadian races, if that is all possible. Will it be the existing rate which I understand to be somewhere in the vicinity of 80 per cent? Will that be the case for foreign races as well?
Yes, Mr. Chairman, that is precisely correct. The rules will be exactly the same as those which govern races presently held in Canada.

Have any Canadian racehorse owners or race-track operators indicated any concern along the lines of the concern expressed by the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley East with respect to whether or not that move would encourage people to bet more on foreign races as opposed to Canadian ones, especially if there is no incentive to ensure that betting is encouraged on Canadian horses as opposed to foreign ones? Have there been any worries to that effect expressed by any of the groups concerned?

Mr. Chairman, that is a difficult question to answer. It is my understanding that track operators and owners, everyone, want this, not so much to make money but to see that the same type of percentage on return stays in Canada.
To return to the question raised by the Hon. Member for Fraser Valley East, that is a concern. I would like to assure the House that we are not looking to a wide proliferation of races; we are talking about prestigious races in the very strict sense of the word.

I gather, then, if I can be so blunt, that this is almost a Kentucky Derby type of provision we are looking at. I
Criminal Code
conclude that there seems to be a great deal of money leaving the country and being bet elsewhere. Perhaps the Minister mentioned that in his opening remarks and I missed it. However, if that is the case, is there any estimate at the present time with respect to the amount of money which leaves Canada and is being bet on races such as the Derby and other races? I recognize that some of this may be illegal right now and it would be difficult to estimate. However, is there any type of estimate at all as to how much money we are losing right now as a result of not having the provisions of this Bill in place at the present time? In other words, how much will we gain as a result of this Bill being enacted? Does the Minister have any idea as to what amount is involved?

Mr. Chairman, there are a couple of sides to the question. There are some benefits which will flow to us in terms of the advertisement and promotion of the sport itself as a result of televising some of the prestigious races which are held outside the country.
In answer to the Hon. Member's first question, obviously what he suggests is illegal and the money leaves the country. There may be people in the industry who may be able to give the Hon. Member an estimate with respect to the amount of money. However, I certainly cannot. I have not even heard an estimate. If we could keep a percentage of that money in the country, under the same type of rules which exist in the racing industry now, then that will be of benefit to us. With respect to how much, I am certainly not able to begin to give an answer.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to ask a question with respect to the integrity of the whole pari-mutuel system. When a better goes to a race-track in Canada and bets, he is betting in the full knowledge that there are certain rules enforced by Agriculture Canada with respect to certain forbidden substances, such as drugs, which a horse can be given. For example, butazolidin is forbidden, and there are others. There are certain standards which we have which is a guarantee the bettor has when he goes to place a bet. If we are to allow Canadian bettors to bet on foreign races which are run on certain conditions in a foreign country, then we are not able to give the same guarantees. Thus, we are in a way short-changing the Canadian bettor, are we not?

Mr. Chairman, no, I do not think that is the case. There is no question that if you bet on a race run outside the country, you are going to bet on a race that is run in a different jurisdiction. However, it should also be recognized that we will not be allowing races to be televised and bet on in Canada unless they are run in accordance with similar or, at least, very strictly supervised rules, similar to what we have in place in Canada. On the one hand, it is a very good question; we cannot totlaly supervise. I also wonder about the odds. Will the pay-out be based on the pay-out shown on the tote board at the

foreign track on the day of the race, or will it be determined and the odds established by the amount bet at the particular track in Canada on the particular race?
The latter is correct. It will not be based on odds and betting outside the country, it will be based on what goes on here.
Regarding prestigious races in Canada at the moment, can a person bet on the Manitoba Derby at a track in Ontario?
Yes.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I want to phrase this question carefully. With the handle at that track, generally speaking one-third of their betting action is from Canada. In this case, because we were not permitted to have the Kentucky Derby at Exhibition Park in Vancouver, it is estimated that approximately $150,000 to $175,000 Canadians went south for bets on the Kentucky Derby. That is one of the good reasons for this legislation; Canadians will not be encouraged to cross the border at Detroit, Buffalo or Washington State to bet on some of the premier races. Was the Minister aware of that?

No, I was not aware of that. I am sure my friends from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell and Nickel Belt, indeed the House in general, are glad to hear those figures. The illustrious Whip of our Party is certainly well-known in racing circles throughout the country. He has a keen interest in this sport as does, I might add, the Queen of our country who has a tremendous racing stable. It is truly a sport of kings and we are very pleased to have this information.

Mr. Chairman, we have established that the return on a dollar bet is 80 cents. That is, by the way, double the return on lotteries. The track and the provincial and federal Governments take 20 cents on the dollar. We all recognize the need to take 20 cents on the dollar. There are certain costs involved with live racing, for example, veterinarian and all sorts of other services which both Governments and the track provide. Given that, why could a greater percentage of the bettor's dollar not be returned to him on foreign races? Why is it essential for the Governments to take the maximum percentages when there are no costs involved for them? All they are doing is simply throwing a picture on the screen and the cashiers are taking the bets.

Mr. Chairman, as a matter of fact, the same amount of supervision will go on. Agriculture Canada officials will be at the track supervising the betting and essentially carrying out the same kind of services they would provide if it was a race being run in Canada. Essentially we will be conducting the same kind of supervision, therefore the costs will be roughly the same.

Not exactly, Mr. Chairman. You do not have the in-stable supervision, the people who do the urine and saliva tests and all the rest. You do not have the circuit patrol. You do not have all these other services. Why do you need to take as big a return when you are not supplying the same amount of services?

First of all, the question is valid but if you look at the scale of things, we are talking about something like 40 races throughout the year. I am told that there are approximately 46,000 races conducted in Canada. The number of races involved in this question is so insignificantly small that to adjust the percentage would not really make any sense. Just doing some quick arithmetic, I think that is one one-thousandth of the number of races conducted in Canada. If you look at it from that point of view, you will find that that is why the percentages will remain the same.

It is just a small point, Mr. Chairman, but in fact races like the Kentucky Derby, the Belmont and the Preakness, many of the breeder's stakes races, are broadcast on TV. So the betting public is sitting at home and they can watch the race. The coverage starts in some cases almost an hour before the race, or at least 30 minutes. People do not really need to go down to the race-track to watch it on the screen, they can pick up the phone and call in their bet.
I come back to the point that these races do not involve the same costs as live races, and therefore I would suggest that a greater return should be given to the bettor.

Again the Hon. Member is talking about a very, very small amount of money. I would also point out that the federal Government does not have any jurisdiction over what goes on provincially in this respect. Given the small number of races we are talking about here, to have a different set of rules or guidelines does not seem to make a lot of sense.

The Government Whip mentioned that $500,000 alone in Canadian bets was placed on the Kentucky Derby. Can you imagine that across the country? Once this facility is provided to the bettor I am sure more people will take advantage of it. If you have 40 prestigious races a year, we can see that we are not talking about nickels and dimes. It is a considerable amount.

Mr. Chairman, if I heard the Government Whip correctly, he did not say $500,000; he said that was the amount bet, of which approximately one-third would be Canadian betting. The Hon. Member makes a good point, but it does cost a certain amount of money to supervise the races anyway. We will take the comments as notice because it is a

valid point. The Government is not looking for ways to make money from this. Just to satisfy my curiosity, what is the rationale for the inclusion of the reference to being able to bet in a building that is within 900 metres of the grandstand, I presume? If you are going on site to bet, you go on site to bet. If you start going to 900 metres to bet, very shortly it will be 1,900 metres and then 6 kilometres. I think we will then end up with betting parlours and turf accountants as they have in Britain.

Mr. Chairman, the 900 metres is stipulated in the Act, and if we wish to change it we will have to come back to the House at which time I am sure the Hon. Member will raise his objections that we are moving further and further away. This is simply for the convenience of the people on the track. The facility has to be on the track. In order to ensure that it is on the track a distance of 900 metres was determined. Rest assured that it cannot be changed by regulation. It is part of the Bill, and in order for it to be changed we will have to come back to the House. I am sure that if we do want it changed the Hon. Member will raise some very legitimate objections at that time. There is no intention to change it. I am just reasurring him that it cannot be changed by regulation, as the Hon. Member knows from looking at the Act.

Mr. Chairman, if I understand this correctly, at the present time the federal Government's portion of a bet is eight-tenths of 1 per cent, or thereabouts, the provincial Government gets 7 cents of every dollar, 12.2 per cent of every dollar goes to the track and horses, and 80 per cent is the return on winnings. The Hon. Member for Nickel Belt has advocated that in the case of foreign races we should have a higher return on investment. I would like to express my disagreement with that to the Minister. We were discussing a while ago how we did not want to create any situation in which there would be no incentive to keep the money here. If we are creating an incentive to bet on horses outside the country, we are doing exactly the opposite of what we were all saying a little while ago. In other words, if you receive a high return on your investment by betting on horses outside the country, you are actually creating a circumstance that most Canadian track and horse owners are not going to be pleased with.
The only portions with which the Minister could be concerned are the eight-tenths of 1 per cent going to the federal Government or the 12.2 per cent going to the track and the horses. I do not think the federal Government would change the 7 per cent provincial share or, if it did, it would not be very well looked upon.
Of the 12.2 per cent which goes to the track and horses from races in Canada, is there a set breakdown of how much goes to
Criminal Code
each? In the case of a race run outside the country, does a portion go to that country in the form of royalties in any way shape or form for the owners of the horses there, or does it simply mean that there is more profit for the track owner here in those cases?

There will have to be some arrangements made between the foreign track and the track here to split fees on whatever basis may be arrived at by the various tracks. I can also advise the Hon. Member that the fee varies from province to province. Some claim 7 cents as the Hon. Member said, and some claim as much as 10 cents.

In the case of betting on races outside the country, am I to conclude that the 12.2 cents that goes to the track and horses in Canada now will be split in some way between the Canadian track and that of the other country? Within the 12 cents?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Resuming debate.

Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to speak to Bill C-42, the Bill to wind up Canagrex. When the Government was first elected we in the agricultural industry had great hopes because of the many promises to the agricultural sectors of the country. In many ways, these were very logical promises and suggestions that anyone who knew something about the agricultural industry would accept and support.
When the Conservatives formed the Government it was our hope that they would fulfil these promises and become the first Government in many years to take agriculture seriously. Many Conservative Members from the West were farmers in the past and had given the kind of voice to agricultural policies which we considered reasonable and worth while. We anticipated that they would be Members who would help farmers and the industry. Although there has been much talk, so far there have been few results from those promises.
The winding up of Canagrex was an unexpected result because the Government did not mention this policy during the election campaign. It is a direct blow to a number of farm groups who believed that they finally had an organization which would do something for the export of farm products. There is no doubt that even during its short tenure, Canagrex demonstrated a very important need for export assistance to the agriculture industry in Canada.
Of course, export assistance is not a new concept because most other sectors in Canada have specific bodies which are used to provide concrete and substantial help when they need it. Assistance to sell Canadian products abroad is common except in the agricultural industry. For instance, the industrial sector has the Export Development Corporation with a budget of approximately $20 bnillion for contingent liabilities with
October 2, 1985

which to provide specific financing to sell particular products in foreign markets. That financing is essentially speculative as the money is lent to the purchasing countries as insurance to help reduce any possible losses that might incur when selling abroad. The producers of military equipment and capital projects operate under another Crown corporation, the Canadian Commercial Corporation. It also provides specific assistance in order to implement projects abroad. Therefore, the idea that Canagrex was new and untried is false. In fact, the dissolution of Canagrex is a direct attack on the ability of the agricultural sector to export its products and develop markets abroad.
I know the Conservative Government in its statement on the wind-up of Canagrex said that other agencies are in place and that people attached to embassies can do the work. However, people have been attached to embassies for the last 25 or 30 years, and they have not succeeded in developing markets that we know can be developed.
Long before Canagrex, it was recognized that the agricultural community needed an instrument to attack the complex world of international trade. In fact, I looked at the history of Canagrex. It is interesting that the idea of an agricultural export agency was brought before this House during the Diefenbaker Government by the Hon. Member for Qu'Ap-pelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) who was the Minister responsible in that Government. He suggested that it was time to put an agricultural export agency in place. This concept was discussed again by the Trudeau Government.
During the short-lived Clark Government, the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) prepared and had in place everything to go ahead with an agricultural export agency. Unfortunately, that Government did not stay in power long enough to put the agency in place. When the concept was brought forward later on, the present Minister of Agriculture actually supported the idea of the export agency. On December 9, 1980, we find on page 5540 of Hansard these words of the present Minister of Agriculture:
We have supported the need for such a structure since 1974. While we were in office the necessary cabinet document had been prepared. What has happened? Has someone canned Canagrex?
Who said that?

The present Minister of Agriculture said that in 1980. During the period of time Canagrex was being debated in the House, the Conservative caucus supported it initially. However, some of the Conservatives friends in the export areas were a little concerned that an agency would cut into the possible development of markets of other agencies. Consequently over several months as the Bill was before the House and Committee, many of changes were made, a number of them at the behest of members of the Conservative caucus from across the country who felt there were some dangers in the Bill. Those dangers were taken out of the Bill and the Bill was passed in 1983.
Canagrex Dissolution Act
To go back to the need for Canagrex, it was quite apparent to people in the agricultural community that some sophisticated method, some agency, some expertise, was needed to develop agricultural markets around the world. An agency was needed to open new horizons for domestic producers in Canada.
When the then Minister of Agriculture suggested such an agency, he got support from all sides oi the House and from all areas of the agricultural industry. That support did not wane as the Bill was developed. It did not disappear after Canagrex was put in place. When this Government presented the windup of Canagrex before this House, the issue rose again. A number of farm groups came forward, stating they were disappointed that they were to lose what they considered, for the first time, to be an agency that dealt specifically with them and worked for them in the export world.
In 1980 the idea of Canagrex finally started to bear fruit. A Bill was placed before the House early in 1981. During the parliamentary debate on Canagrex, as I mentioned, particular concern was expressed by some Opposition Members over one clause. I want to zero in on that clause because it seemed to be the basis of the opposition.
Opposition Members said that they feared legislation would be used by the Government to interfere in normal commercial trade. Others felt instruments already in place were being duplicated. During the time this Bill was before Committee, a number of amendments were brought forward. Those amendments were put in place to ensure the agency received plenty of guidance and scrutiny, both from the private and the public sectors; that it would engage in trade only on a state to state basis in the development of markets and that it would not interfere in any private development of trade. Other things were passed in the Bill.
That kinds of corporations have a tendency to grow like Topsy was another concern. People say they will do only a certain amount, but the net result is they do considerably more. They start at $12 million and before you know what happens, they hit $60 million. To be sure that kind of thing did not happen, that the agency did not invade the private sector and raise concerns, very sophisticated control was put in place. No Crown corporation was every established with as many controls or with as much authority and guidance as was Canagrex. Everything was done to make sure that Canagrex did not cut into the trade of the private sector or into any other market sector which might possibly be affected. Everything was done to make sure it would be financially responsible and that it would not expand beyond the references given within the Bill. In fact the Auditor General was given the authority to call a comprehensive audit at any time he felt that it was necessary, so there was no concern about the financial responsibility of this particular organization. It was the first time in Canadian legislation that any corporation or agency was so well controlled or financially regulated by the Government. The Auditor General felt that no other organization or agency was quite as well as scrutinized as Canagrex. It was a bit of a shock, not only to those of us in the House but to those in the

Canagrex Dissolution Act
agricultural community, to find that it was to be wound down, after a substantial investment and after an auspicious start on the part of the corporation, in that it was starting to do some work and starting to sell products.
Mr. Glenn Flaten, who was chairman of the 11-member Board of Directors of Canagrex, had been the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and a member of numerous other agriculture-related associations and boards. He had an interest in ensuring that the board and its staff had control over what went on. He paid close attention to what happened in the debates in the House of Commons. He knew the concerns of Members of Parliament and of agricultural organizations. He was an excellent choice for chairman. The board worked very closely with the executives. Its members travelled and established many contacts. They worked particularly hard and particularly quickly. The Bill was passed in May, 1984, and toward the end of the following summer the money was put in place for the organization. In fact, an August 29 press release indicated that a $15 million line of credit had been arranged with a Cuban organization for sales and that many other contacts had been made, but of course time was running out. It is interesting to note that in September, when the new Government came into power, it immediately withheld the money voted by Parliament for this organization. As the company was beginning to operate and to show its value, the money was not available. Then, on November 8, 1984, without any consultation or examination, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) indicated in his economic statement that Canagrex was to disappear. Many farm organizations felt that they had been betrayed. They were consulted and made recommendations in favour of the development of Canagrex to help them sell their products. Suddenly, without examination, without a fair trial and without consultation, the Minister of Finance cancelled it, making a farce of the parliamentary system and of the consultative system. The Conservative Government allowed agriculture to drop to third or fourth place in Canadian trade. The Government is trying to develop trade, but it has refused to finance and has withdrawn from an active role in the one agency which could have helped around the world.

Mr. Speaker, it is interesting that the House allows us an opportunity to learn more about our country. As I looked at the legislation affecting Canagrex and as I listened to my colleague's speech, I could not help but wonder whether there was a parallel. Is there a parallel between the agency which is now being eliminated by the Conservative Government and the Canadian Wheat Board in terms of their function as between Canadian producers and potential markets elsewhere in the world?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the Hon. Member's question, in that it gives me an opportunity to expand somewhat on the kind of structure which has been in place.
The Canadian Wheat Board is an agency of the Government and Canagrex is a Crown corporation. Technically they are somewhat different. As far as their mandates are concerned, there is much similarity. The Canadian Wheat Board has the responsibility to go out and sell grains and to develop markets to ensure an even flow of grain, as much as possible. Of course other factors are affected as well. Canagrex had eliminated from its responsibility grains which were under the auspices of the Canadian Wheat Board and other products already under other marketing boards. However, it had responsibilities in terms of any other product which could be considered an agricultural one. Honey, apples and other products which came under other boards were not affected. It could work with any of those boards to develop markets overseas. It was aimed at developing the agricultural market and working with existing marketing and producer boards. There is a marginal parallel. It was intended to help those boards.
I suppose one of our most sophisticated marketing boards is the Canadian Wheat Board. It does not need help in developing its market, although it can be prodded on occasion. I see that the Minister is present; we will prod him when it is necessary. The Canadian Wheat Board has very sophisticated marketing in place, and it can help those boards which do not.

Mr. Speaker, I listened very attentively to the Hon. Member's speech. It was very interesting when he said that the Conservative Party had made an about-face. I find it strange that it would do this. I guess it was the first time in the last half hour that I heard about Conservatives changing their mind on a major issue.
What does the Hon. Member think could have possessed the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) to change his mind from his good intentions in 1979 and shortly thereafter? Does he think that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), "Mike the Knife" as he is affectionately known to all of us, had anything to do with this twisting of opinion which seems to have happened? Once again the Tories have contradicted themselves. Would he like to comment on that?
[DOT] (WOO)
We, of course, have to surmise the answer to that question. It is very uncharacteristic for the Conservatives to change their mind, as we all know.
They haven't done it in the last half hour.

The Minister was no doubt in favour of an export marketing agent for agriculture, and the Party was in favour also, otherwise the Minister, who had been a Minister in the Clark Government, would not have brought it forward. I would think that to some extent the decision to cancel Canagrex was based more on the fact that the Conservatives had publicly opposed it during committee hearings, and across Canada, and felt that they had to follow through in some way even if, in the process of opposing it, they had done a lot of good with improvements and making it a very responsible agency. I have to give Hon. Members of the Conservative Party who were in committee at that time a lot of credit for picking out faults and getting the Government to change those areas about which they were concerned. We did not always
October 2, 1985

agree with those changes but if that was their concern, they did well.
I feel, therefore, that the cancellation of Canagrex is purely political. It is really a disaster because it is done without any basis. They did not look at how well it could do and how much good it could do for the country.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Are there any more questions or comments? Debate.

Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure to enter this debate, although I do feel that the Canagrex situation has been discussed many times. However, people are still wondering what happened to it. I think it boils down very simply to the fact that we had an agency which was spending somewhere in the area of $6 million and had $50 million worth of orders. I do not think we could call that very efficient.
One of the reasons I am entering into the debate today, Mr. Speaker, is because I am troubled by some of the things I have heard today. I believe this Government has been one of the most sensitive Goverments to the needs of farmers that this Parliament has seen for many years. I have a list in my hand, and I do not wish to go over them all for the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), of some 90 achievements of this Government since September 4, 1984.
That must be plain paper you have in your hand.

I can read them, Mr. Speaker. This Government has spent somewhere in the area of $1.53 billion since the election on agricultural issues. I am not too sure we have the time to go through all of the excellent programs the Government has put forward.
Go for it.

Perhaps I will read a few of the programs this Government has put into effect. As early as October 1, 1984, a $60 million federal-provincial prairie livestock drought assistance program was announced by the Minister. A few days later on October 17, 1984, $181,340 was granted through the Agricultural and Rural Development Subsidiary Agreement to Brookside Farms, B.C. On November 2, 1984, a $123 million final payment under the Western Grain Stabilization Program was announced. On November 5, 1984, the Minister of Agriculture announced that up to $627,286 in funding for projects under Agriculture Canada's new Crop Development Fund. Then, of course, the Minister showed his concern for the agriculture community. Many farmers were facing foreclosures due to mismanagement by the previous Government which had told farmers to go out and borrow, borrow, borrow and grow, grow, grow, and we will sell it. That is the reason, Mr. Speaker, that

the Canadian farmers are in the difficulties in which they are today. Some farmers took the advice of the Liberal Government over the past number of years and now they find themselves unable to pay back those tremendous debts incurred during that period of time. However, the Minister of Agriculture, as early as November 5, two months after the election, put a moratorium on FCC loans which helped the farmers at that time and, of course, he has done it again very recently.

That's nonsense, and you know it.
The Government showed some compassion and bought the crops of the grape growers.
Let them eat grapes.
I know it hurts. I am only down to number nine and I have 89 more to go.
What about the western grain stabilization?

We can talk a little about the western grain stabilization, if the Hon. Member likes, Mr. Speaker. Bill C-25 was the Western Grain Stabilization Act. The previous Government sat by for many years. It did not have the guts to put the stabilization program through. At that time it would have been much simpler to have a stabilization program in Canada than at the present time because each province had to develop its own programs in order to keep its farmers on the land. The federal Government sat back and said, "Let the provinces do it". Now we have a system whereby every province is top loading. It is almost impossible in some cases to get a national agreement. However, our Minister and this Government have decided that we are going to have an agreement. It will be the best agreement that can possibly be achieved at this present time. It would have been a lot easier had the previous Government moved on that type of legislation. We would not then be in the situation we are today.
I will just highlight some of the programs which had been announced by this Government. On November 30, 1984, a $3.3 million emergency cash advance under the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act was made available. On December 3, 1984, it was announced that land was being purchased for the construction of a $10 million research centre on pest control in London, Ontario. On December 7, 1984, $200,000 worth of evaporated milk was donated by Canadian dairy farmers to relieve the starvation in Ethiopia. Four per cent over the year.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

recall that on June 19, 1985, the former Minister of Fisheries and Oceans opened a $ 16-million research facility at Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu, Quebec. That is just one of the things that have been done. There are many more but-

Mr. Speaker, that is certainly a very important question coming from a very honourable Member who represents a rural riding. I am sure he keeps very close contact with his constituents.
I am finding, and I am sure the Hon. Member is finding the same thing, that once we explain the Government policy on agriculture to our constituents, they are very, very pleased with what we are doing. They realize that we have a very tough job to do. We are going through a time that has been one of the toughest times for many, many years.
