Mr. Speaker, I am of course very pleased to be taking part in this debate, but, with your permission, I would like to digress somewhat before starting my comments. In answer to the question I asked earlier, my hon. colleague opposite said that the Government's achievements included a research centre in Saint-Jean, which cost $16 million. I might remind my hon. friend that this project is merely the implementation phase of a project we had already developed. If my time had not run out, I would have asked him what happened to the centre for Victoriaville, which was cancelled outright. This was a project worth $16 million.
The Conservatives did that. Incredible!

That being said, Mr. Speaker, I would like to get back to Bill C-42, which is actually a very short Bill, since it contains only one section I find important and that is Section 3, which says: The Corporation is hereby dissolved. One section, and there you have the whole Bill. However, I think it is a real tragedy to see something that had become a veritable institution, and that was the result of an unprecedented round of consultations, die like this.
Canagrex was the result of consultations with all the main parties concerned, without a single exception. Throughout those consultations, a number of concerns and issues were raised. However, I beleive that anyone who took the trouble to really understand and analyze the potential of Canagrex understood that the Corporation would have a positive impact on the entire agro-food industry. Bill C-42 has proved to be a golden opportunity to see the true colours of this administration.
For the first time since September 4, 1984, we can see what kind of policy this Government has with respect to agriculture. Of course, they have tried to camouflage their problems with all sorts of mechanisms and strategies. They were supposed to make a number of decisions and then postponed them, giving the impression or inferring or saying that consultations were not yet completed and a decision would be delayed. I am of course referring to the dairy policy, which was supposed to be known or made public on August 1. This is the first time we have been able to grasp something tangible and significant about this Government's true intentions and its true face. Without going very far back into the past, it is interesting to note how this Government has been administering the country and what kind of image it gave the people, particularly those in the agro-food industry. Of course I am more familiar with the commitments and promises made by different spokesmen to the agricultural community throughout Quebec. For instance I have in mind a man who should be taken at his word-at least I would think so since I am referring to the Minister of Public
Works, the Hon. Roch La Salle-who stated in rather colourful words before the largest gathering of farmers in Longueuil: We in the Conservative Party have learned that a man must eat if he wants to go on living. As you can appreciate, it was his way of saying that agriculture was a basic industry, that it was one of the Government's priorities, and he went on to explain what would be done in that sector. That was the principle which, in a way, summed up the electoral commitments to the food producing industry.
Some of those commitments were indeed very specific and very formal. Among other things, and I mentioned this earlier, the Minister of Public Works put his signature to a $13 million symbolic cheque. Well, Mr. Speaker, they are telling you today that they spent over $1 billion to promote agriculture, but they just could not spare the $13 million for pork producers.
They also promised a long term dairy policy. Knowing as we do that this strategic sector is the mainstay of Quebec's agriculture, we can readily imagine the anxiety and concern of producers who have now been waiting for this famous long term policy since August 1 last. It has been put off, practically hidden as a result of what appears to be a tactic of further consultations, but it seems quite clear that we should be prepared for rather drastic cut-backs in that sector.
And then the matter of stabilization about which they said: We will do absolutely nothing! We will not tamper with that. We will consult you and, after reaching a consensus, we will go ahead. We all know what has happened to stabilization. Indeed my colleague opposite was again patting himself on the back a moment ago when he said: This is something fantastic, something of which we are quite proud, something which has been in the interest of Canadian food producers. Unfortunately that is not my opinion and since my opinion might be viewed as biased, or demagogic as my colleague from Levis (Mr. Fontaine) said earlier today in a statement under Standing Order 22, because it seems that we do not have the research facilities of Members opposite-
But I think that he then opened the door for me so that I could indicate to you ... not the personal view of the Hon. Member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif), but what those who live and develop in close contact with the Quebec farm industry think that you have done since you came to power on September 4, 1984.
Concerning the dairy policy, I should like to quote from an article which was published in La terre de chez nous and which was entitled "Western cereals preferred to milk. Ottawa has broken its promise". I quote:
Brian Mulroney's Conservative Government has broken another of its election promises. It is already certain that the long term dairy policy will not be announced on August 1.
Here is another quote under the following heading:
"Quebec farm industry will go through a difficult year following the major gains made in 1984. The producers' indebtedness has increased by 25 per cent-

Dairy producers would like Wise-

These are newspaper quotes which clearly indicate what we are aware of Quebec farm producers in general and dairy producers in particular. The Government should not brag about its performance, for the report I have just made of the situation in Quebec is far from good.

The Federation of Hog Producers will sue the Federal Government.

Let us go on to another matter about which the Government seems also to be very proud, the stabilization measure, Bill C-25. I would invite the Quebec Members to speak up on this issue, if there are any here.
This is what we find in the newspaper La terre de chez nous of August 23, 1985, and I quote:
Quebec farmers protest that they have been betrayed-he also denounces the 58 Conservative Members of Parliament, "these men and women who have abandoned us at the first opportunity and who did not stand up to oppose passage of Bill C-25".

Let us look at other newspaper cuttings. I shall deal with them more quickly and give only their titles: "Stabilization Bill-Systematic Hypocrisy in Ottawa." These are the comments of Mr. Jacques Proulx, the President of the UPA. 1 am not the one to say all this.

These are the comments of a Member of the Parti quebecois with conservative leanings!

Here is another comment from Mr. Garon: "Bill C-25 will not be accepted in Quebec."
As concerns the Crow's Nest, if I refer to the Longueuil meeting-

Point of order, Mr. Speaker. 1 have been listening with interest to the Hon. Member as I am trying to improve my French. I would like to thank the Hon. Member for his speech. However, he has been referring to the Crows-nest Pass freight rate, Bill C-25, and a number of other subjects, and I am just wondering precisely what he is trying to get at and if the rule of relevance applies in this debate.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The point raised by the Hon. Member is, of course, well taken by the Chair. However, prior speakers in this debate have spoken in general terms on matters of agriculture. I made a comment prior to the speech of the Hon. Member and 1 hope he, like other Members in this House, speaks to the Bill as much as possible.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. If the Hon. Member had listened to my remarks, I think he would not have voiced that objection.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-42 deals with Canagrex. Canagrex was created for the purpose of promoting internationally the Canadian agro-food industry. To my knowledge, agro-food activities cover milk, apples, as well as all other products referred to in my earlier clippings.
Anyway, Mr. Speaker, I was coming back to Bill C-42 but you will allow me, before I do so, perhaps more specifically and with relevance to Bill C-42 ... I would like, with your permission, to simply refer to a last clipping headed: "Farm bankruptcies" This is how I relate that to Bill C-42.
"Farm bankruptcies-figures and human impact" Over the last year, there has been a 20 per cent increase in the number of farms sold through TON because of bankruptcy. While we look at bankruptcy data, we also consider the social, environmental and human damage caused by bankruptcies.
Mr. Speaker, Canadian farming has reached a point where it is essential, absolutely necessary that government should help, support and invest in agriculture. Unfortunately, the

October 2, 1985
Canagrex Dissolution Act
farming industry does not have the ability to pay, the capacity to create organizations which would promote its products overseas or on foreign markets. That was indeed the role of Canagrex. That was the purpose, the ultimate goal of that corporation and it is now being destroyed through Bill C-42. That purpose would have been, in difficult periods such as the one Canadian farming is now going through, to open up markets, to help producers faced with tremendous difficulties make ends meet, and hope that at some point in time they will increase their production and thereby make their operations more viable.
Canagrex is and was more specifically in my view an essential tool, for a number of reasons but especially because Canadians, as we all know, do have a very large country with a relatively small population, unfortunately. We are 25 million Canadians. But because of this large country of ours, we have the opportunity, the possibility and the power to develop our farms, to expect to profit from those extremely large farms, to produce, to foster, to develop products which unfortunately our population cannot absorb in all cases, as seen from that little test.
So we must hope, if we want to develop farming, to take our rightful place on foreign markets, to take our place among countries which are privileged with having a much larger population than ours. But the demise of Canagrex, this Government's move to abolish it, mean that suddenly, they are flushing down the drain that absolutely vital tool needed for the Canadian economy really to expand.
We also are in a situation where people talk about competition, and productivity, where everyone agrees that the agrofood industry is no exception, that there are incredible economies of size to be sought out, unbelievable economies to be expected by investing in research, which directly results in increased productivity, and increased production. Canagrex was the tool designed to find markets for those surpluses, and of which clearly the economy has an obvious need.
I feel that the Canagrex move is a direct, unacceptable and most cruel attack against small family farms. Of course, those who have millions of dollars invested in that industry can afford to have a salesman, a sales force, public relations teams to sell their products. However, the small farmers or the families who need every minute of their time to make both ends meet cannot invest in the exploration for new markets and cannot put new funds into marketing. And this was precisely the purpose of Canagrex. And this Government which said it was in sympathy and wanted to support agriculture dissolves Canagrex after just about everybody has recognized its effectiveness and the fact that it could have been a necessary tool.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would say that Bill C-42 is by a long way the best proof that the concerns and the awareness of this Government are to a much larger extent related to multinationals, banks, big corporations than to small family
businesses. This Government wants to apply to the agri-food industry the rules of capitalism and competition to the extent that this will result in countless bankruptcies and breakups, and larger corporations will gradually take over the small family businesses which in my opinion are the true fabric of our agriculture, especially in Quebec.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Questions or comments. The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom).

I should like to ask a question, Mr. Speaker.
I agree with many things which the Hon. Member has just said, but I wonder why the Liberal Government took so long to set up Canagrex. I know Mr. Whelan quite well and I agree with the project, but the Liberal party was in power for 20 years, Mr. Trudeau was there for 15 years, Mr. Whelan for 12 or 13 years. Why did it take so long to set up an organization such as Canagrex, considering the fact that it began operating 18 months ago?

My hon. colleague knows perfectly well, Mr. Speaker, since he probably took part in the debate, that the Canagrex Bill did not come out of the blue. Consultations were held for several months and even years, and I know, because I was here in the House, that in 1979, the first step was made, and at that time, if 1 remember correctly, the Progressive Conservatives, the party opposite, had expressed a number of objections, so that the realization of this concept, which could have come in the eighties, had to be postponed. But the Canagrex Corporation was a fact, and it was generally recognized, and I would like to take this opportunity to recall some of what was said by my hon. friend of the New Democratic Party who said earlier that the Auditor General had to admit that this Crown corporation was one of the best administered and best organized and one likely to generate the best results.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), for a supplementary.

I would like to ask a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I approve of Canagrex. But why did the Liberal Party wait twenty years before proceeding to its creation? You referred to consultations that lasted several months, I agree with that, but why wait twenty years? Because you must not forget that Mr. Pearson won the 1963 elections and Mr. Trudeau those of 1968. Producers experienced so many problems. So why did it take twenty years? I know the Liberal Party is slow, but my God!
The Liberal Party is infinitely faster than the New Democrats.

More dynamic also. The New Democrats will never be in office.
October 2, 1985

Here is my answer. Parts of it lie in the question itself, Mr. Speaker. One must go back twenty years. My colleague said that was twenty years ago. The premise of his question seems to me somewhat odd since twenty years ago, we were not even capable of a production such as the one we had in 1982-83, and the problems Quebec's and Canada's agriculture experienced in the 80s cannot be compared to those of the 60s. I think that in reality the appropriateness of that corporation appeared in the 80s. Even though there might have been a delay of one, two or three years, the parliamentary system being what it is, I do not think it is surprising that the corporation was established under our administration. We can see how slowly things evolve under the new administration.

Mr. Speaker, I have a comment and some questions. I listened carefully to what the Member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Tardif) said. I thought he may have spoken a little about how Canagrex duplicated the services that are otherwise available within Government and private enterprise, about the fact that we sell 40 per cent of our products of private enterprise abroad, about how Canagrex only succeeded to the small extent that it did because it was able to extend credit, and about how it competed with the private enterprise that opened the Japanese, Polish and Chinese markets.
Instead of speaking of those things, the Member spoke of how the federal Government is now interfering in Quebec-I forget the term he used-by offering Quebec, under the tripartite plan, 3 per cent of its domestic sales if it wishes to come into the stabilization plan. I do not know how he believes that the Government is somehow hurting Quebec by offering to give it money for its scheme. I do not know how the Member can talk about getting additional $13 million from the Agricultural Stabilization Act when the people who would receive that money were already protected by a Government-funded bipartite scheme paying their expenses as well as a specialized wage. I believe that last year they got approximately $28 a hog and they still wished to have the $6.75 per hog which came out of the Agricultural Stabilization Act.
Does the Member for Richmond-Wolfe think it is fair for a Government which must look after the whole of Canada to give hog farmers in Quebec the stabilization plan for the 2.1 million hogs in the Quebec market on top of the very rich plan which is in the Quebec arena at the present time?

What I would like for Quebec finally is an amount similar to that Western Canada is getting in the first place. Secondly, you raised three points: To start with, you said a number of factors and circumstances affected the sale of farm products overseas. I would like to say that, in terms of farm business, your notion of profit must be wrong, for if it were to be taken to the letter, you would just have caused about 80 percent of the farm businesses to go bankrupt. This is an area where the Government has no choice
Canagrex Dissolution Act
but to get financially involved. It has to support Canagrex, and even if Canagrex had done nothing else but to provide for its management needs, there was a justification for it, and its activities should be allowed to go on.
The problems of agriculture are so desperate that the Government has to support it. You mentioned stabilization schemes. The answer is dead simple: if you have two programs, with a net result of $10 for one and $1.50 for the other, knowing you as I do, you are bound to opt for the $10 one. That is what we have now. In Quebec, we have a stabilization program which is very generous to producers. There is no damn sense in what you guys are saying, that is: get rid of your program and get in on ours.
The third aspect is hog production. On the matter of hogs, since you are making so much fuss about equity, I will tell you that hog producers are taxpayers just like you, they pay the same taxes as you do. Why should they be deprived of their fair share, the same share as Ontario and Western Canada got, and which they are denied for bureaucratic reasons? That amount is due, the Minister of Public Works pledged it, and it should be paid.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate my hon. colleague on an excellent speech. He is clearly able to defend the interests of Quebec in this House, Mr. Speaker. I would like to ask him if I was right in understanding that the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. La Salle), the Hon. Member for Joliette, during the election campaign, did indeed promise to give $13 million to the producers of Quebec and even wrote out a cheque, and that cheque was made out of rubber, as they say in my riding. Is that indeed what the Minister of Public Works did, and if so, how can it be said that such a Minister, and such a Government are indeed interested in agriculture when they keep backing off from their promises? Did I understand correctly?

That is indeed what happened and there was I believe ample coverage of that matter in the newspapers. The present Minister of Public Works who was in a generous mood, signed his name-he was not the honourable at the time-Roch La Salle, on a $13 million cheque. He did much more than that, because that is one problem. It is a 13 million problem. But there is another one, a $450,000 problem, the sheep problem. There has been less talk about the smaller producers, because there are fewer of them to speak up and defend their interests. But on that day, in Longueuil, the Minister of Public Works also signed his name on a $450,000 cheque.
Those sheep producers now have to go to court to get what is rightfully theirs. And hog producers have done exactly the same thing, they had to institute proceedings against the Government in order to get back those $13 million. This is quite unacceptable in my opinion! It is unacceptable that this problem should have been allowed to drag on for so long and

October 2, 1985
Canagrex Dissolution Act
the reason we were given is that if we paid those $13 million, it would bring about a more or less favourable decision from the United States.
The Minister even recognized in Committee that he had consulted the Americans about the Stabilization Act but that he had not take into account the demands of the province of Quebec. Therefore, the Minister who was obviously feeling very uncomfortable and unhappy about paying those $13 million, because it would affect a decision yet to be taken . . . So, that decision was taken and it was in fact acceptable. We asked the question: Why not pay those $13 million? We were given another reason. Because of that, unfortunately, those to whom that money belonged have to go to court to get what is rightfully theirs.

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of State (Canadian Wheat Board)):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is an interesting afternoon in the House. Anyone who was watching this debate-although I am not sure anyone would want to watch what has been going on here-would have to conclude that the Government is made up of a bunch of shysters-

Let me repeat that anyone listening to what the Opposition has been saying about us would think that no Government Member who is a farmer would dare to go home on the weekend to visit our constituents because the farmers are totally upset with us and at variance with everything we do.
Certainly there are things we would like to do as a Government that we are unable to do for various reasons. However, we have been able to accomplish some of our goals and I think that the Opposition would be more credible if it would acknowledge some of our achievements. We realize that the Opposition will condemn us on most matters but surely they must recognize that we have accomplished some of our goals.
The Opposition may object to our stance on Canagrex but those Members who were here for the part of the debate leading up to the creation of Canagrex will know that there were some major problems associated with that Bill. None of us dealing with the Bill at that time could say anything against the necessity for advertising or financing and promotion of agricultural products. Canada is more dependent than the United States or the European Community on exports of agricultural products for the well-being of its farmers. We recognized that but we also disagreed with a major proposal in the Bill that Canagrex be authorized to own and further process products. We supported the provision of the Bill dealing with the financing and promotion of agriculture and would have been happy to support it on that basis. Perhaps, once Canagrex had a reputation and the expertise was developed in the agency it could have been expanded further as
needed. However, Canagrex should not have been created with so many extra powers.
When we took office we took a different approach with respect to Canagrex. Again, let me point out some of the action our Government has taken. The Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) says that we have done nothing.
No, I did not. I said that those things would have been done anyway.

Let me finish. He said that we have done nothing that has required initiative on the part of the Government. That is entirely not the case. Let me explain some of the initiatives our Government has taken. Without our initiative there would not have been an interim payment under the Western Grain Stabilization Act which pumped some $250 million into the Province of Saskatchewan. I have stated in the House previously that this initiative was supported by the Opposition and we appreciate that. It benefited western farmers. It is wrong for the Opposition to say that we have done nothing that has required initiative on our part. It is simply not the case that the action we have taken is a result of ongoing Government programs.
Furthermore, for the first time, we made use of the provisions under the meat import law which resulted in a reduction in the amount of meat coming into the country. Regardless of what is said, the amount of meat coming to Canada from offshore will be smaller this year than it was in 1984 as a result of the initiatives taken by this Government.
The Opposition talks about the November 8 economic statement. The Minister of Finance found over $100 million to use as a rebate on farm fuel. Surely Members opposite will not stand in the House to say that they are opposed to that measure and state that objection to farmers in their ridings. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) froze the seaway tolls. That was an initiative of the Government that saved producers a significant amount of money. That initiative will benefit farmers.
Last spring, we took the initiative to study the sugar beet industry in this country. It was an initiative that resulted in an interim measure to allow producers in Alberta, Manitoba and Quebec to plant sugar beets. Although we were unable to reach an agreement in Alberta, and Alberta producers did not plant sugar beets, there would have been no sugar beet industry at all without that initiative.
We made a campaign commitment to establish a procedure by which tobacco farmers could establish a marketing board. That was one of the first pieces of legislation passed in the House, in fulfilment of that commitment. However, listening to the Opposition, one would think that we have done absolutely nothing for agriculture and are totally abandoning that sector. That is simply not the case and I think the Opposition would have much more credibility and add a great deal to the demeanor of the House if they would give us credit for some of the initiatives we have taken. The Opposition may criticize the Government for not taking enough action or not taking it soon
October 2, 1985

enough and give us its suggestions but it should not be totally negative and disregard everything we have accomplished. It does not do the Opposition, the House or the agricultural industry any good at all-

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Minister blames us for all the sins of the world, but I would like to remind him that the purpose of today's debate is to allow Members of Parliament to speak on Canagrex and not to give the Government credit it takes for itself.
I would urge him to speak on the Bill and not on what he calls in other-

Mr. Speaker, obviously the Opposition does not want to hear about those positive steps we have taken on behalf of farmers. However, if it is fair for a Member of the Opposition to take 20 minutes to do nothing but berate the Government about matters which have nothing to do with Canagrex, at least it should be fair for a Member of the Government to take some time to demonstrate what the Government has done for agriculture. I suggest that it is just common courtesy and good manners, if nothing else.
Let me make some remarks about Canagrex. We all recognize that one of the reasons for the creation of Canagrex was that farmers need as much export earnings as possible. We have taken some initiatives in terms of agricultural financing. As of yesterday, a program under the Export Development
Canagrex Dissolution Act
Corporation was established to assist in short-term financing with respect to bulk agricultural products. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) is presently in the Soviet Union conducting trade promotion in that part of the world. I was pleased to be invited to the Soviet Union in June. That country is our largest customer for grain. We have not abandoned Canadian farmers in their efforts to export products. I repeat that the Opposition is wrong in using this Bill as a basis for saying that the Government has totally abandoned agriculture. That is certainly not the case. I see that you are signalling that my time is almost up, Mr. Speaker.
One of the other things Canagrex was attempting to do was to provide more advertisement and more market intelligence. We are currently doing that through increased awareness around the world via our embassies. That is the kind of thing going on and about which Hon. Members need to know in terms of this Government taking its responsibilities and seeing that we continue to export as farmers. Canadian farmers have a tremendous record around the world. We are very well thought of.
Hear, hear!
That is one thing on which we all agree. I shall conclude on that happy note.
